newsitem.title: GERMANY: Holocaust survivors seek pay-out from Allianz.
newsitem.headline: Holocaust survivors seek pay-out from Allianz.

text.p: Holocaust survivors on Monday visited the corporate headquarters of German insurance group Allianz AG and said it was high time insurance companies paid up on policies sold during the Nazi era.

Margret Zentner and Marta Cornell, who both survived the Nazi terror in World War Two, are part of a mass U.S. legal action against 16 European insurers, claiming the companies cheated victims of Nazi persecution out of billions of dollars.
"Fifty years is too long," Zentner said, adding that she hoped for a quick resolution to the proceedings.
A spokesman for Allianz said there was no case to answer on formal legal grounds, but said the insurer was morally obliged to find a speedy solution.
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said both the Zentner and the Cornell families had bought insurance policies with Allianz or Allianz subsidiaries before the war.
Zentner's policy was supposed to be paid out when she turned 21 or married, but the plaintiffs say the policy was actually paid out to the (Nazi) SS in 1942 and the policy cancelled.
Nazi Germany required insurers to hand over Jewish life insurance policies under the racist laws that culminated in the mass murder of six million European Jews.
As Zentner was in Theresienstadt concentration camp at the time, she was unable to do anything to stop the pay-out and after the war Allianz refused to pay out on the policy, she said.
Zentner's lawyer Edward Fagan said he expected the proceedings in the U.S. to be concluded quickly.

The suit against the insurance companies, which includes insurers in Germany, Austria, Italy, Switzerland and France, would not be allowed to drag on because of the age of the 20,000 plaintiffs who make up the class action suit, he said.
Fagan would not give exact figures as to the sum involved in the suit, but the amount is estimated to be in the billions of dollars.
He said interest and other charges would have to be added on to the pay-outs and claimed Allianz would have profited from the money obtained from the Jews.

As such, the plaintiffs should be allowed share in Allianz profits, which means the payout could be in Allianz shares, Fagan said. He recommended his clients attend the next Allianz shareholder meeting.
He also accused Allianz of trying to gain access to 600 files and documents relating to damages claims by Holocaust victims.
Fagan alleged Allianz had sought information about claims from regional offices to co-ordinate damages claims, and said it was alarming that the defendants were trying to look at plaintiff's files.
The Allianz spokesman denied the accusations and said the insurer was only trying to help damages applicants meet their claims.
Attempts to locate documents were only necessary when the necessary papers could not be furnished from the Alliance archives, Allianz said.

Allianz said it was running a 24-hour telephone hotline to inform the descendants of victims of Nazi persecution about the insurance policies of their ancestors. The company said it would help descendants register their claims.
The Allianz spokesman told the two plaintiffs that the company bore a moral responsibility in this case, as Allianz was part of the system during the Third Reich.
Allianz said it was in contact with the plaintiff's lawyers and that it wanted to find a solution as quickly as possible.
